subject: DI02000021

intro_text.en: Unit 5 of Engineering Mathematics: the complex number and its Argand diagram, algebra and powers of i, conjugate, modulus and inverse, argument and polar form, De Moivre's theorem with roots, and the square root of a complex number together with the cube roots of unity. Twenty fully solved numericals, each linked to a card.

h.en: 1.1 Why a new kind of number

body.en:
The problem

The equation x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, because no real number squares to −1. Engineering needs the missing root: a circuit's characteristic equation, a rotation matrix and a differential equation all produce it.

The definition

Introduce i = √(−1), so i² = −1. A complex number is z = a + ib, where a and b are real.

  • a is the real part, written Re(z)
  • b is the imaginary part, written Im(z)
  • if b = 0 the number is real; if a = 0 it is purely imaginary

Examples

3 + 4i has Re = 3 and Im = 4. The number −5i is purely imaginary, and 7 is real. There is no order: 3 + 4i is neither bigger nor smaller than 1 + i.

Common mistake

Writing Im(3 + 4i) = 4i. The imaginary part is the real number 4; the i is part of the symbol, not of the number b.

h.en: 1.2 Powers of i follow a cycle of four

body.en:
The cycle

PowerValue
i¹i
i²−1
i³−i
i⁴1

After four steps the values repeat, so iⁿ depends only on the remainder of n divided by 4.

Worked examples

i¹⁵: 15 = 4 × 3 + 3, so i¹⁵ = i³ = −i.

i²²: 22 = 4 × 5 + 2, so i²² = i² = −1.

Why it works

i⁴ = (i²)² = (−1)² = 1, so every group of four powers multiplies by 1 and can be dropped.

Common mistake

Dividing by 4 and using the quotient instead of the remainder. It is the remainder that picks the row of the table.

Plotting

A complex number a + ib is drawn as the point (a, b): a along the real axis, b along the imaginary axis. The plane is called the Argand diagram or the complex plane.

Distance and direction

The length of the arrow from the origin is the modulus |z| = √(a² + b²), and the angle it makes with the real axis is the argument θ.

Useful pictures

  • The conjugate a − ib is the reflection in the real axis.
  • Multiplying by i turns the arrow 90° anticlockwise.
  • Adding two numbers completes a parallelogram.

Common mistake

Plotting a + ib at (b, a). Real part first, imaginary second - exactly like (x, y).

The rule

Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match: a + ib = c + id means a = c and b = d. One complex equation carries two real equations.

Worked example

If (x + 2) + (y − 3)i = 5 + 4i, then x + 2 = 5 and y − 3 = 4, so x = 3 and y = 7.

With a product

For (x + iy)(2 + i) = 7 + 4i, expand to (2x − y) + (x + 2y)i = 7 + 4i, then solve the pair 2x − y = 7, x + 2y = 4.

Common mistake

Comparing only the real parts and forgetting the imaginary equation - half the information is then unused.

Rule

Add (or subtract) the real parts together and the imaginary parts together: (a + ib) ± (c + id) = (a ± c) + i(b ± d).

Worked example

(5 − 2i) + (−3 + 4i) = (5 − 3) + (−2 + 4)i = 2 + 2i.

Subtraction: (5 − 2i) − (−3 + 4i) = 8 − 6i.

Geometric meaning

On the Argand diagram the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram built on the two arrows, exactly like vector addition.

Common mistake

Adding 3 + 4i and 1 + 2i as 4 + 6i² - the parts combine, they are not multiplied.

Rule

Expand like brackets and then replace i² by −1: (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac − bd) + i(ad + bc).

Worked example

(3 + 2i)(4 − 5i) = 12 − 15i + 8i − 10i² = 12 − 7i + 10 = 22 − 7i.

Special products

  • (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b², always real and positive
  • (1 + i)² = 2i, a result worth remembering for powers
  • i(a + ib) = −b + ia, a rotation through 90°

Common mistake

Leaving the answer as 12 − 7i − 10i². The i² must be replaced by −1 before the answer is in the form a + ib.

Method

Multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator. The denominator then becomes real, and the answer splits into real and imaginary parts.

Worked example

(1 + 2i)/(3 − 4i): multiply by (3 + 4i)/(3 + 4i). The denominator is 3² + 4² = 25, and the numerator is (1 + 2i)(3 + 4i) = −5 + 10i.

So the answer is (−5 + 10i)/25 = −1/5 + (2/5)i.

Why multiply by the conjugate

(a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b² has no i in it, so the denominator clears in one step. This is the same trick that rationalises a surd.

Common mistake

Multiplying by the denominator itself instead of its conjugate, which leaves the i in place.

h.en: 2.4 Working with powers by repeated squaring

body.en:
The trick

For small powers, square instead of expanding: (1 + i)² = 2i, so (1 + i)⁴ = (2i)² = −4 and (1 + i)⁶ = (1 + i)⁴(1 + i)² = (−4)(2i) = −8i.

Reading off the parts

From −8i the real part is 0 and the imaginary part is −8.

When to prefer De Moivre

Repeated squaring is quick for powers up to about 8. For larger powers, or when the answer must be a single number, De Moivre's theorem in section 5 is safer.

Common mistake

Squaring a sum term by term: (1 + i)² is 2i, not 1 + i² = 0.

Definition

The conjugate of z = a + ib is z̄ = a − ib: same real part, opposite imaginary part. On the Argand diagram it is the mirror image in the real axis.

Properties

  • z + z̄ = 2a, which is twice the real part
  • z − z̄ = 2bi, which is twice the imaginary part
  • z · z̄ = a² + b², always real and never negative
  • the conjugate of a sum is the sum of the conjugates, and the same for a product

Worked example

For z = 3 − 4i, the conjugate is 3 + 4i, and z z̄ = 9 + 16 = 25.

Common mistake

Changing the sign of the real part instead of the imaginary part.

Definition

The modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) is the distance of the point from the origin, and it is always a non-negative real number.

Worked example

|3 − 4i| = √(9 + 16) = 5. For z = −1 + i√3, |z| = √(1 + 3) = 2.

Properties

  • |z₁ z₂| = |z₁| |z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|
  • |z|² = z z̄ = a² + b²
  • |z| = 0 only for z = 0

Common mistake

Dropping the i before squaring, or forgetting the square root at the end. The answer is a plain number, not a complex one.

Formula

z⁻¹ = 1/z = z̄/|z|². Multiplying z by this gives 1, so it really is the inverse.

Worked example

For z = 3 − 4i, |z|² = 25 and z̄ = 3 + 4i, so z⁻¹ = (3 + 4i)/25 = 3/25 + (4/25)i.

Check

(3 − 4i)(3 + 4i)/25 = 25/25 = 1, so the answer is right.

Common mistake

Writing 1/z = 1/a + 1/(ib). The reciprocal of a complex number is not the sum of the reciprocals of its parts.

h.en: 3.4 Division seen as multiplication by the inverse

body.en:
Two views of the same step

Dividing z₁ by z₂ means multiplying by z₂⁻¹ = z̄₂/|z₂|², which is exactly the 'multiply top and bottom by the conjugate' rule of section 2.

Worked example

(2 + i)/(1 − i): the conjugate of the bottom is 1 + i and |1 − i|² = 2. The numerator becomes (2 + i)(1 + i) = 1 + 3i, so the answer is (1 + 3i)/2 = 1/2 + (3/2)i.

Useful consequences

|z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| and the conjugate of a quotient is the quotient of the conjugates - both follow at once from this view.

Common mistake

Forgetting to divide the whole numerator by |z₂|² after multiplying.

Definition

The argument θ is the angle the arrow makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise. The principal value lies between −π and π.

Finding it

Compute α = tan⁻¹|b/a| first, then fix the quadrant: first quadrant θ = α, second θ = π − α, third θ = −(π − α), fourth θ = −α.

Worked example

For z = −1 + i√3, α = tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3 and the point is in the second quadrant, so θ = π − π/3 = 2π/3.

Common mistake

Taking tan⁻¹(b/a) and stopping there. The calculator only returns values between −π/2 and π/2, so quadrants 2 and 3 always need the correction.

The form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ, where r = |z| and θ = arg z. It is the same number written by length and direction instead of by coordinates.

Worked example

For z = 1 + i: r = √2 and θ = π/4, so z = √2 cis (π/4).

Converting both ways

  • Cartesian to polar: r = √(a² + b²), θ from the quadrant rule
  • Polar to Cartesian: a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ

Common mistake

Mixing the two forms in one answer, such as √2(cos 45° + i) - either write cos and sin, or write r cis θ.

Third quadrant

For z = −3 − 3i: r = √(9 + 9) = 3√2 and the point is in the third quadrant, so θ = −(π − π/4) = −3π/4 (the same angle as 5π/4).

Hence z = 3√2 cis (−3π/4).

Back to Cartesian

4 cis (π/3) = 4(cos 60° + i sin 60°) = 4(1/2 + i√3/2) = 2 + 2√3 i.

Choosing the angle

Both −3π/4 and 5π/4 describe the same point. The principal value, inside (−π, π], is the one normally marked and the one De Moivre works with most cleanly.

Common mistake

Using r sin θ for the real part. cos goes with the real axis, sin with the imaginary axis.

h.en: 4.4 Multiplication and division in polar form

body.en:
Rules

  • multiply: r₁ cis θ₁ × r₂ cis θ₂ = r₁r₂ cis (θ₁ + θ₂)
  • divide: r₁ cis θ₁ ÷ r₂ cis θ₂ = (r₁/r₂) cis (θ₁ − θ₂)

Multiplying multiplies the lengths and adds the angles; dividing divides the lengths and subtracts the angles.

Example

(2 cis 30°)(3 cis 50°) = 6 cis 80°, and (6 cis 80°) ÷ (3 cis 50°) = 2 cis 30°, which returns the original number.

Why it matters

This is the reason phasors work in AC circuits: the product of two phasors is another phasor whose angle is the sum.

Common mistake

Adding the moduli or multiplying the arguments. It is the other way round.

Statement

(r cis θ)ⁿ = rⁿ cis (nθ) for every integer n. In cosine form, (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ.

Reading it

Raise the modulus to the power and multiply the argument by the power. That single line replaces pages of binomial expansion.

Why it is true

Multiplying by r cis θ adds θ to the argument, so repeating the multiplication n times adds θ exactly n times. Induction makes the argument precise.

Routine

  1. Write z in polar form: find r and θ.
  2. Apply the theorem: modulus rⁿ, argument nθ.
  3. Bring nθ back into the principal range and finish in a + ib if asked.

Common mistake

Raising the angle to the power as well. It is n times θ, not θⁿ.

Example 1

(1 + i)⁸: r = √2 and θ = π/4, so the answer is (√2)⁸ cis (8 × π/4) = 16 cis 2π = 16.

Example 2

(1 − i√3)⁶: r = 2 and θ = −π/3, so the answer is 2⁶ cis (−2π) = 64 cis 0 = 64.

Reading the answer

When nθ lands on a whole multiple of 2π the answer is real and positive; a half turn makes it real and negative; a quarter turn makes it purely imaginary.

Common mistake

Adding 2π to the modulus instead of to the argument, or forgetting that a negative angle is allowed.

Formula

The n roots of z are r^(1/n) cis ((θ + 2kπ)/n) for k = 0, 1, …, n − 1. They sit on a circle of radius r^(1/n), equally spaced.

Worked example

The fourth roots of 16 = 16 cis 0 are 2 cis 0, 2 cis (π/2), 2 cis π and 2 cis (3π/2), that is 2, 2i, −2, −2i.

Why equally spaced

Each root is the previous one multiplied by cis (2π/n), so the angle steps by 360°/n - here 90°.

Common mistake

Giving only the principal root. An n-th root question expects n answers, unless the question says 'principal value'.

Example 1: a power

(√3 + i)⁴: r = 2 and θ = π/6, so the answer is 16 cis (2π/3) = 16(−1/2 + i√3/2) = −8 + 8√3 i.

Example 2: solving z³ = 8

Write 8 = 8 cis 0, then z = 2 cis (2kπ/3) for k = 0, 1, 2, giving 2, 2ω, 2ω².

The three roots of any cube

The roots of z³ = a³ are a, aω and aω², where ω and ω² are the complex cube roots of unity. Recognising this saves the full calculation.

Common mistake

Solving z³ = 8 and giving only z = 2. The real cube root is one of three complex roots.

title.en: 6. Square Roots and the Cube Roots of Unity

body.en:
Setting it up

Let √(a + ib) = x + iy. Squaring gives x² − y² = a and 2xy = b, and also x² + y² = r = √(a² + b²). Adding and subtracting the first and third give the formula.

The formula

√(a + ib) = ±[√((r + a)/2) + i·sign(b)·√((r − a)/2)], where r = √(a² + b²) and sign(b) is + for b > 0 and − for b < 0.

Worked example

For 3 + 4i: r = 5, so the real part is √(8/2) = 2 and the imaginary part is √(2/2) = 1. Hence √(3 + 4i) = ±(2 + i).

Check

(2 + i)² = 4 + 4i − 1 = 3 + 4i, so the answer is right.

Common mistake

Reporting only the positive root. Every non-zero complex number has two square roots, opposite in sign.

Example 1

For 8 − 6i: r = 10, so the real part is √(18/2) = 3 and, since b < 0, the imaginary part is −√(2/2) = −1. The answer is ±(3 − i).

Example 2

For −5 + 12i: r = 13, so the real part is √(8/2) = 2 and the imaginary part is √(18/2) = 3. The answer is ±(2 + 3i).

A shortcut

For a number of the form a + ib with a² + b² a perfect square, the root has integer parts - try small values first, then confirm by squaring.

Common mistake

Using r = a² + b² without the square root, which doubles every answer.

Solving z³ = 1

Write 1 = 1 cis 0. Then z = cis (2kπ/3) for k = 0, 1, 2, giving three roots:

  • 1 (k = 0)
  • ω = −1/2 + i√3/2 (k = 1, argument 120°)
  • ω² = −1/2 − i√3/2 (k = 2, argument 240°)

The picture

All three lie on the unit circle and are 120° apart, with 1 on the real axis. Their sum is zero, which is the symmetry you can see in the diagram.

Common mistake

Writing ω = 1/2 + i√3/2. The real part is negative: −1/2.

Three facts

  • ω³ = 1
  • 1 + ω + ω² = 0, so ω² = −1 − ω
  • ω and ω² are conjugates, and each is the square of the other

Worked example

Simplify (1 + ω − ω²)³. Replace ω² by −1 − ω: 1 + ω − ω² = 1 + ω + 1 + ω = 2(1 + ω) = −2ω².

Cubing: (−2ω²)³ = −8ω⁶ = −8, because ω⁶ = (ω³)² = 1.

Why the sum is zero

1 + ω + ω² = (ω³ − 1)/(ω − 1) = 0 for ω ≠ 1, since ω³ = 1.

Common mistake

Substituting ω = 1 to simplify. ω is a specific complex number, not 1; only ω³ is 1.

h.en: 7.1 Five steps for any complex-number question

body.en:
The routine

  1. Write the given number in the form asked for - a + ib or r cis θ.
  2. For a power or a root, convert to polar form first.
  3. Apply De Moivre, or the conjugate trick for a quotient.
  4. Return to a + ib and simplify the angle to the principal range.
  5. State modulus and argument separately if the question asks for them.

Marks and layout

Most schemes award marks for the polar form, the value of rⁿ and the final angle separately, so show the conversion even if the arithmetic is short.

Time saver

Learn (1 + i)² = 2i, i³ = −i and the three cube roots of unity by heart; between them they cover a large share of the questions.

h.en: 7.2 Mistakes to avoid, and quick checks

body.en:
Six recurring errors

  1. Im(3 + 4i) written as 4i instead of 4.
  2. Using tan⁻¹(b/a) without the quadrant correction.
  3. Replacing i² by +1 instead of −1.
  4. Raising the argument to the power instead of multiplying it.
  5. Giving one square root or one cube root when two or three exist.
  6. Writing ω = 1 when simplifying expressions in ω.

Quick checks

Verify a square root by squaring it, verify a quotient by multiplying back, and verify a power by comparing the modulus (rⁿ) with the size of the answer.

Why does a complex power sometimes come out real?

Because the new argument nθ is a multiple of π, so the sine term vanishes and only the cosine term survives.

Reduce each power modulo 4: 21 = 4 × 5 + 1, so i²¹ = i¹ = i.

36 = 4 × 9, so i³⁶ = (i⁴)⁹ = 1, because any power of i⁴ is 1.

The sum is i + 1 = 1 + i, which is already in the standard form a + ib with a = 1 and b = 1.

h.en: Practice 2. Find x and y if (x − 2) + (y + 5)i = 3 − 2i.

body.en:
Equate the real parts: x − 2 = 3, so x = 5.

Equate the imaginary parts: y + 5 = −2, so y = −7.

Answer: x = 5, y = −7. One complex equation gives two real equations, which is why two unknowns can be found.

h.en: Practice 3. For z₁ = 4 − 3i and z₂ = −2 + 5i, find z₁ + z₂ and z₁z₂.

body.en:
Sum: (4 − 2) + (−3 + 5)i = 2 + 2i.

Product: (4 − 3i)(−2 + 5i) = −8 + 20i + 6i − 15i² = −8 + 26i + 15.

So z₁z₂ = 7 + 26i, and both answers are in the standard form a + ib.

Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate 4 + i.

Denominator: (4 − i)(4 + i) = 16 + 1 = 17.

Numerator: (2 + 3i)(4 + i) = 8 + 2i + 12i + 3i² = 5 + 14i.

The quotient is (5 + 14i)/17 = 5/17 + (14/17)i.

h.en: Practice 5. Find the conjugate and modulus of z = 6 − 8i.

body.en:
The conjugate flips the imaginary part: z̄ = 6 + 8i.

The modulus is √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10.

Check: z z̄ = 36 + 64 = 100 = |z|², which confirms both numbers.

h.en: Practice 6. Express −1 − i in polar form.

body.en:
Modulus: r = √(1 + 1) = √2.

The point (−1, −1) is in the third quadrant, and α = tan⁻¹(1) = π/4, so θ = −(π − π/4) = −3π/4.

Hence −1 − i = √2 cis (−3π/4), equivalently √2 cis (5π/4) with a positive angle.

h.en: Practice 7. Express 2 + 2√3 i in polar form.

body.en:
Modulus: r = √(4 + 12) = 4.

The point is in the first quadrant and tan θ = 2√3/2 = √3, so θ = π/3.

Therefore 2 + 2√3 i = 4 cis (π/3), and converting back gives 4(1/2 + i√3/2) = 2 + 2√3 i, which checks the answer.

h.en: Practice 8. Evaluate (1 − i)⁶ using De Moivre's theorem.

body.en:
Polar form: r = √2 and θ = −π/4, so 1 − i = √2 cis (−π/4).

De Moivre: (√2)⁶ cis (6 × (−π/4)) = 8 cis (−3π/2).

cos(−3π/2) = 0 and sin(−3π/2) = 1, so the value is 8i - purely imaginary.

Modulus r = √(1 + 3) = 2 and θ = tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3, so z = 2 cis (π/3).

Then z⁶ = 2⁶ cis (6 × π/3) = 64 cis 2π.

A full turn brings the point back to the real axis, so the answer is 64.

Square first: (1 − i)² = 1 − 2i + i² = −2i.

Square again: (−2i)² = 4i² = −4.

So (1 − i)⁴ = −4, a real number, which matches De Moivre with the angle −π making a half turn.

h.en: Practice 11. Find the square roots of 8 + 6i.

body.en:
Here a = 8, b = 6 and r = √(64 + 36) = 10.

Real part: √((10 + 8)/2) = √9 = 3. Imaginary part: √((10 − 8)/2) = 1, positive since b > 0.

The roots are ±(3 + i). Check: (3 + i)² = 9 + 6i − 1 = 8 + 6i.

h.en: Practice 12. Find the square roots of −15 − 8i.

body.en:
Here a = −15, b = −8 and r = √(225 + 64) = 17.

Real part: √((17 − 15)/2) = 1. Imaginary part: −√((17 + 15)/2) = −4, negative because b < 0.

The roots are ±(1 − 4i). Check: (1 − 4i)² = 1 − 8i + 16i² = −15 − 8i.

h.en: Practice 13. Solve z³ = 1 and verify that the three roots add to zero.

body.en:
Writing 1 = 1 cis 0, the roots are cis (2kπ/3) for k = 0, 1, 2, that is 1, ω = −1/2 + i√3/2 and ω² = −1/2 − i√3/2.

Sum of the real parts: 1 − 1/2 − 1/2 = 0. Sum of the imaginary parts: √3/2 − √3/2 = 0.

So 1 + ω + ω² = 0, as expected from (ω³ − 1)/(ω − 1) = 0. Each root also has modulus 1 and they are 120° apart.

h.en: Practice 14. Simplify (1 + ω − ω²)³, where ω³ = 1 and 1 + ω + ω² = 0.

body.en:
Use ω² = −1 − ω: then 1 + ω − ω² = 1 + ω + 1 + ω = 2(1 + ω).

But 1 + ω = −ω², so the bracket equals −2ω².

Cubing: (−2ω²)³ = −8ω⁶ = −8(ω³)² = −8, because ω³ = 1.

h.en: Practice 15. Find all cube roots of 27.

body.en:
Write 27 = 27 cis 0, so the cube roots are 3 cis (2kπ/3) for k = 0, 1, 2.

That gives 3, 3ω and 3ω², with ω = −1/2 + i√3/2.

Explicitly: 3, −3/2 + (3√3/2)i and −3/2 − (3√3/2)i. Each has modulus 3 and they are 120° apart; cubing any of them returns 27.

q.en: Simplify i¹⁵.

a.en:
Write the exponent as 4 × 3 + 3, so i¹⁵ = (i⁴)³ · i³.

Since i⁴ = 1 and i³ = −i, the value is 1 × (−i) = −i.

The powers of i repeat every four, so only the remainder on division by 4 matters.

q.en: Find x and y if (x + 2) + (y − 3)i = 5 + 4i.

a.en:
Equate the real parts: x + 2 = 5, so x = 3.

Equate the imaginary parts: y − 3 = 4, so y = 7.

Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts agree, which is why one equation gives two real conditions.

q.en: Add and subtract 5 − 2i and −3 + 4i.

a.en:
Add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately: (5 − 3) + (−2 + 4)i = 2 + 2i.

Subtract: (5 + 3) + (−2 − 4)i = 8 − 6i.

On the Argand diagram the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram on the two arrows.

q.en: Multiply (3 + 2i)(4 − 5i).

a.en:
Expand: 12 − 15i + 8i − 10i².

Use i² = −1, so −10i² = +10: the expression becomes 12 − 7i + 10.

The answer is 22 − 7i, with real part 22 and imaginary part −7.

q.en: Divide (1 + 2i) by (3 − 4i).

a.en:
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate 3 + 4i.

Denominator: (3 − 4i)(3 + 4i) = 9 + 16 = 25. Numerator: (1 + 2i)(3 + 4i) = 3 + 4i + 6i + 8i² = −5 + 10i.

So the quotient is (−5 + 10i)/25 = −1/5 + (2/5)i.

q.en: Find the conjugate and the modulus of z = 3 − 4i.

a.en:
The conjugate keeps the real part and flips the imaginary part: z̄ = 3 + 4i.

The modulus is the distance from the origin: |z| = √(3² + (−4)²) = √25 = 5.

Check with the product: z z̄ = 9 + 16 = 25 = |z|², as the theory requires.

q.en: Find the modulus and argument of z = −1 + i√3.

a.en:
Modulus: |z| = √(1 + 3) = 2.

The point (−1, √3) lies in the second quadrant, and α = tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3.

For the second quadrant θ = π − α = π − π/3 = 2π/3.

So z = 2 cis (2π/3).

q.en: Express 1 + i in polar form.

a.en:
Modulus: r = √(1 + 1) = √2.

The point (1, 1) is in the first quadrant, so θ = tan⁻¹(1) = π/4.

Hence 1 + i = √2 (cos π/4 + i sin π/4) = √2 cis (π/4).

q.en: Express −3 − 3i in polar form.

a.en:
Modulus: r = √(9 + 9) = √18 = 3√2.

The point is in the third quadrant and α = tan⁻¹(1) = π/4, so θ = −(π − π/4) = −3π/4.

Hence z = 3√2 cis (−3π/4), the same angle as 5π/4 if a positive argument is preferred.

q.en: Evaluate (1 + i)⁸ using De Moivre's theorem.

a.en:
Polar form: 1 + i = √2 cis (π/4).

De Moivre: (√2 cis π/4)⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis (8 × π/4) = 16 cis 2π.

Since cos 2π = 1 and sin 2π = 0, the answer is 16.

q.en: Evaluate (1 − i√3)⁶.

a.en:
Modulus √(1 + 3) = 2, and the fourth-quadrant angle is θ = −π/3, so z = 2 cis (−π/3).

De Moivre gives 2⁶ cis (−6π/3) = 64 cis (−2π).

A full turn gives cos(−2π) = 1 and sin(−2π) = 0, so the answer is 64.

q.en: Evaluate (√3 + i)⁴.

a.en:
Modulus √(3 + 1) = 2 and θ = tan⁻¹(1/√3) = π/6, so z = 2 cis (π/6).

Then z⁴ = 16 cis (4π/6) = 16 cis (2π/3).

Now cos 2π/3 = −1/2 and sin 2π/3 = √3/2, so the answer is −8 + 8√3 i.

q.en: Find the square roots of 3 + 4i.
Find the square roots of 8 − 6i.

a.en:
a = 8, b = −6, so r = √(64 + 36) = 10.

Real part: √((10 + 8)/2) = √9 = 3. Since b < 0 the imaginary part is negative: −√((10 − 8)/2) = −1.

The roots are ±(3 − i). Check: (3 − i)² = 9 − 6i − 1 = 8 − 6i.

q.en: Find the square roots of −5 + 12i.

a.en:
a = −5, b = 12, so r = √(25 + 144) = 13.

Real part: √((13 − 5)/2) = √4 = 2. Imaginary part: √((13 + 5)/2) = √9 = 3, positive because b > 0.

The roots are ±(2 + 3i). Check: (2 + 3i)² = 4 + 12i − 9 = −5 + 12i.

q.en: Solve z³ = 1 and write all three roots.

a.en:
Write 1 = 1 cis 0. By De Moivre the roots are z = cis (2kπ/3) for k = 0, 1, 2.

k = 0 gives 1; k = 1 gives cis (2π/3) = −1/2 + i√3/2 = ω; k = 2 gives cis (4π/3) = −1/2 − i√3/2 = ω².

All three lie on the unit circle at 120° intervals, and their sum is 1 + ω + ω² = 0.

q.en: Simplify (1 + ω²)³, where ω is a complex cube root of unity.

a.en:
From 1 + ω + ω² = 0 we get ω² = −1 − ω, so 1 + ω² = −ω.

Cubing: (−ω)³ = −ω³.

Since ω³ = 1, the value is −1.

q.en: Simplify (1 + ω − ω²)³.

a.en:
Replace ω² by −1 − ω: 1 + ω − ω² = 1 + ω + 1 + ω = 2 + 2ω = 2(1 + ω).

But 1 + ω = −ω², so the bracket is −2ω².

Cubing: (−2ω²)³ = −8ω⁶, and ω⁶ = (ω³)² = 1, so the value is −8.

q.en: Find all fourth roots of 16.

a.en:
Write 16 = 16 cis 0, then the roots are 16^(1/4) cis (2kπ/4) = 2 cis (kπ/2) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3.

k = 0 gives 2, k = 1 gives 2i, k = 2 gives −2 and k = 3 gives −2i.

They lie on the circle of radius 2 at 90° intervals, so each is the previous one multiplied by i.

q.en: Find the real and imaginary parts of (1 + i)⁶.

a.en:
Use (1 + i)² = 2i, so (1 + i)⁶ = (2i)³ = 8i³.

Since i³ = −i, the value is −8i.

Therefore the real part is 0 and the imaginary part is −8: the number is purely imaginary.

q.en: What is a complex number?

a.en: A number of the form a + ib with a and b real; a is the real part and b the imaginary part.

q.en: Why do we need complex numbers?

a.en: Because equations such as x² + 1 = 0 have no real root, and rotations, AC circuits and vibrations are described most simply with them.

q.en: What is the value of i²?
What is the imaginary part of 3 + 4i?

a.en: 4 - the imaginary part is the real coefficient b, not 4i.

q.en: How many complex roots does z³ = 1 have?

a.en: Three: 1, ω and ω², all on the unit circle 120° apart.

q.en: Can two complex numbers be compared as larger or smaller?

a.en: No - the complex numbers have no order, although their moduli can be compared.

q.en: Define the conjugate of z = a + ib.

a.en: z̄ = a − ib, the reflection of z in the real axis.

q.en: What is z z̄?

a.en: a² + b² = |z|², a non-negative real number.

q.en: Define the modulus and give its geometric meaning.

a.en: |z| = √(a² + b²), the distance of the point (a, b) from the origin.

q.en: Write the inverse of z in terms of the conjugate.

a.en: z⁻¹ = z̄/|z|², valid for every z ≠ 0.

q.en: How is division of complex numbers performed?

a.en: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, so the denominator becomes real.

q.en: How do you find the argument of a complex number?

a.en: Take α = tan⁻¹|b/a| and then adjust for the quadrant: θ = α, π − α, −(π − α) or −α.

q.en: State De Moivre's theorem.

a.en: (r cis θ)ⁿ = rⁿ cis (nθ) for any integer n.

q.en: How do you multiply two numbers in polar form?

a.en: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments: r₁r₂ cis (θ₁ + θ₂).

q.en: How many n-th roots does a non-zero complex number have?

a.en: Exactly n, equally spaced on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

q.en: What are the cube roots of unity?
Why is 1 + ω + ω² = 0?

a.en: Because ω³ = 1 and ω ≠ 1, so 1 + ω + ω² = (ω³ − 1)/(ω − 1) = 0.

q.en: How do you find the square root of a + ib?

a.en: Let it be x + iy; use x² − y² = a, 2xy = b and x² + y² = r to obtain x = √((r + a)/2) and y = ±√((r − a)/2).
